Shifting stress to 'REPORT' or 'WE' would redirect the focus of the message to what is being submitted or who must submit it, demonstrating that stress choice actively shapes meaning.

workedExamples.title: Planning and Structuring a Five-Minute Presentation
workedExamples.problem: A student must deliver a five-minute presentation on the topic 'Social media is more harmful than beneficial for university students.' Show how to plan and structure this presentation using the introduction–body–conclusion framework, and estimate appropriate time allocation for each section.
steps: Step 1 – Calculate the total word budget. At a comfortable pace of approximately 130 words per minute for a formal presentation, a five-minute talk contains roughly 130 × 5 = 650 words. This sets a realistic scope: you cannot cover five main points in 650 words; two or three is appropriate.

Step 2 – Plan the Introduction (target: ~1 minute / ~130 words). Open with an attention-getter: a striking statistic or rhetorical question, e.g., 'Did you know that the average university student spends over four hours a day on social media — more time than they spend in lectures?' State the thesis clearly: 'Today I will argue that, on balance, social media does more harm than good for university students.' Preview the main points: 'I will look at two areas: its impact on academic performance and its effect on mental health.'

Step 3 – Plan the Body (target: ~3 minutes / ~390 words). Develop two main points, each with a claim, evidence, and explanation. Point 1 (academic performance): social media multitasking reduces concentration; cite relevant research or examples. Point 2 (mental health): comparison culture and cyberbullying increase anxiety and depression rates among students. Use signpost language between points: 'Having considered academic performance, I now turn to mental health…'

Step 4 – Plan the Conclusion (target: ~1 minute / ~130 words). Summarise both main points briefly: 'I have shown that social media undermines both academic focus and emotional wellbeing.' Restate the thesis in new words: 'For university students, the costs of heavy social media use outweigh the benefits.' Close with a memorable final thought or call to action: 'The next time you reach for your phone between classes, consider whether that scroll is working for you or against you.'

Step 5 – Review the structure for balance and flow. Check that the body accounts for roughly 60% of total time, that each point is distinct and does not repeat another, and that the conclusion introduces no new arguments.
workedExamples.answer: The five-minute presentation should be structured as: Introduction (~1 min) with an attention-getter, thesis, and preview; Body (~3 min) with two clearly signposted main points supported by evidence; Conclusion (~1 min) with a summary, restated thesis, and memorable close. At 130 words per minute, the total script is approximately 650 words, confirming that two main points is the right scope.

workedExamples.title: Designing a Readable Presentation Slide
workedExamples.problem:
A student writes the following text on a single PowerPoint slide:
'Social media platforms such as Instagram, Twitter, Facebook, and TikTok have been found in multiple studies conducted between 2015 and 2023 to significantly reduce the attention span of university students, increase rates of depression and anxiety, promote unhealthy body image through constant comparison with curated online profiles, and reduce the overall quality and quantity of sleep due to late-night screen use.'
Apply the 6×6 rule to redesign this slide so it communicates the same information effectively.
steps: Step 1 – Count the problems with the original slide. The original is a single 68-word sentence on one slide. It has no visual hierarchy, no bullet points, and would appear as a dense block of text that is impossible to read at a glance. It violates the core principle that slides support speech rather than replacing it.

Step 2 – Identify the key ideas hidden in the sentence. Reading carefully, there are four distinct harms: (1) reduced attention span, (2) increased depression and anxiety, (3) unhealthy body image from comparison, (4) poorer sleep due to screen use.

Step 3 – Apply the 6×6 rule. Maximum 6 bullet points, maximum 6 words each. Draft the redesigned slide:
  Title: 'How Social Media Harms Students'
  • Shortens attention span (studies 2015–2023)
  • Raises depression and anxiety rates
  • Promotes unhealthy body comparison
  • Disrupts sleep via late-night screens
That is 4 bullets, each under 6 words. The title is the claim; the bullets are the evidence categories.

Step 4 – Consider further visual improvement. Replace or supplement the bullet list with a simple two-column visual: 'Harm | Effect on Student Life', or use a single icon beside each bullet. Use a font size of at least 24pt for body text and 36pt for the title so text is legible from the back of the room.

Step 5 – Confirm what the speaker adds verbally. The full detail — the specific platforms, the date range, the mechanisms — is delivered orally. The slide provides the skeleton; the speaker adds the flesh. This division of labour is what makes a presentation more engaging than a written essay read aloud.
workedExamples.answer: The redesigned slide carries a clear title ('How Social Media Harms Students') and four concise bullets (attention span, mental health, body image, sleep), each under six words and in at least 24pt font. All specific detail is delivered verbally. This satisfies the 6×6 rule, ensures legibility, and maintains the audience's focus on the speaker rather than on reading dense text.

quiz.question: A lecturer says 'I did NOT say she stole the money.' Then repeats the sentence stressing a different word each time. What aspect of spoken English is this demonstrating?
options: Intonation patterns signalling question versus statement
Sentence stress shifting the focus and implied meaning of an utterance
Word stress determining the correct pronunciation of individual words
Pace variation to maintain audience interest
quiz.explanation: Placing stress on different words in the sentence ('NOT', 'I', 'she', 'stole', 'money') changes what is being contrasted or emphasised, demonstrating how sentence stress controls the communicative focus of an utterance.

quiz.question: According to the 6×6 rule, which of the following slides is most appropriately designed?
options: One slide containing two 80-word paragraphs explaining the causes of inflation
One slide with a bold title and four bullet points of five words each
One slide with twelve bullet points covering every sub-point of the presentation
One slide displaying the speaker's full script so nothing is forgotten
quiz.explanation: The 6×6 rule recommends a maximum of six bullets per slide and six words per bullet; four bullets of five words each is well within this limit, keeping the slide readable and uncluttered.

quiz.question: During the question-and-answer session after a presentation, an audience member asks a long and unclear question. What is the best strategy for the presenter?
options: Answer immediately to avoid appearing unprepared, even if the question was not fully understood
Paraphrase the question back to the questioner to confirm understanding before answering
Decline to answer and move to the next question to save time
Admit you did not understand and ask the audience for help
quiz.explanation: Paraphrasing the question confirms the presenter has understood correctly, shows respect for the questioner, and gives the presenter a moment to organise a thoughtful response.

quiz.question: In a seminar discussion, a student wants to disagree with the previous speaker's argument without being dismissive. Which response best illustrates correct seminar etiquette?
options: 'That is completely wrong and shows you haven't read the material.'
'Whatever — let me just tell everyone my own point instead.'
'I take your point about funding cuts; however, the evidence suggests student numbers also play a role.'
'I agree with everything you said, and I have nothing to add.'
quiz.explanation: Acknowledging the previous speaker's point before introducing a contrasting view is an example of hedging and constructive disagreement, which is central to respectful seminar participation.
